title: Negative-capacitance bitline dielectric makes the bitline vanish electrically
idea: Ideal result: a bitline with zero capacitance, so every femtofarad of cell charge becomes signal. Closest achievable: line the bitline-to-plate spacer with a thin stabilized HZO negative-capacitance layer in series with the parasitic, so effective Cbl drops 2-3x while staying hysteresis-free in the small-signal range.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) rises from ~0.1 to ~0.25, allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes, fact 7).

title: Frequency-addressed wordlines replace row decoders with tuned resonators
idea: Ideal result: no decoder at all; the address is broadcast and the right row answers. Each sub-wordline driver gets a tiny BEOL LC or bulk-acoustic resonator tuned to one of 64 frequencies; a global line carries a tone burst and only the matching resonator's rectifier fires its driver, with a 2-level predecode covering 64x64 rows.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): a decoder tree becomes one broadcast line plus passive filters stacked above the drivers; ~30% smaller row-decoder stripe.

title: Microwave dispersive readout senses cells without draining them
idea: Ideal result: a read that costs nothing and leaves the bit untouched. Borrowing qubit readout, make each bitline segment part of a GHz resonator; a storage node gating a tiny varactor shifts the resonance, and a picowatt probe tone reflected from the line reveals the bit with no charge sharing and no restore.
why: Destructive read and CV^2 energy (facts 8, 10): no restore cycle and no full-swing bitline; target <0.5 pJ per useful bit versus ~5.9 pJ.

title: Inductive charge sloshing reads and restores bits adiabatically
idea: Ideal result: the cell's charge travels to the sense node and returns with zero loss. A shared BEOL spiral inductor between a cell group and the sense node makes the transfer resonant: full charge moves in half an LC period (instead of lossy charge sharing), is sampled at the peak, and swings back to the cell on the next half-period.
why: Facts 1, 8, 10: removes the charge-sharing loss and most restore energy; signal approaches full Cs voltage instead of ~10% transfer ratio, 2-4x lower read energy.

title: Pulse-echo bitline reads a whole column of gain cells at once
idea: Ideal result: one probe reads every cell on a line simultaneously. Treat a long bitline as a transmission line where each non-destructive gain cell loads it with a state-dependent impedance step; a 10 ps edge launched from the end returns a time-encoded echo train decoded by one comparator plus time-to-digital converter.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and overfetch (fact 8): one sensing front end per 256+ cells instead of one SA per bitline pair, suited to column-streaming AI reads.

title: Ferroelectric-stored offset trim lets sense amps resolve 5 mV
idea: Ideal result: a sense amp with zero offset. At wafer test, each latch's mismatch is measured and written as a polarization state into a small FeFET in its tail or body-bias path, so the offset stays cancelled with no trim registers, fuses or periodic calibration.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): required bitline signal falls from ~20 mV to ~8 mV, allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines, cutting SA stripes (fact 7) by up to 40%.

title: BEOL oxide-transistor preamps chop bitlines into tiny segments
idea: Ideal result: every cell has its own amplifier. Closest: one IGZO thin-film preamp in the BEOL above each 16-cell bitline segment converts the local charge into a current on a global bitline, so the silicon SA sees a large current signal instead of a millivolt swing.
why: Facts 1, 2, 7: local Cbl falls ~10x, enabling ~1 fF capacitors and 3D tiers whose short local bitlines need no per-tier silicon sense amp.

title: Two-threshold sensing turns every read into a retention health check
idea: Ideal result: refresh only the bits that are truly about to fail. Every Nth activation, the SA stripe fires against a second, offset reference that flags cells whose signal is within 30% of failing; the controller logs those rows for faster refresh and stretches refresh for the healthy majority.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3): measures the leakage tail in the field instead of guarding for it; 60-80% fewer refreshes, reclaiming most of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Stochastically doped nanowire decoders discovered rather than drawn
idea: Ideal result: a decoder that needs no lithographic precision. Grow wordline-select nanowires with random axial doping segments that form random but unique codes against a coarse address mesh; at test, map which code selects which row into a table and accept a few percent unusable rows.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4) and periphery area (fact 7): replaces EUV-pitch decoders with self-assembled ones at cell pitch.

title: Single-transistor-type periphery built from the array's own vertical channels
idea: Ideal result: periphery that costs zero extra masks. Design sense amps, drivers and decoders entirely from the array's vertical-channel access transistor, with a few gate lengths set by etch depth, dropping the separate high-k metal-gate planar CMOS flow for core periphery.
why: Capital and masks (fact 4): removes ~10-15 periphery mask steps and 1-2 EUV layers; periphery and array share one process.

title: Paired banks swap bitline charge instead of dumping it
idea: Ideal result: bitline swings cost nothing because charge is borrowed and returned. When a bank precharges, its high bitlines connect through a shared bus to a second bank's bitlines that are about to precharge, so half that bank's charge comes from the first bank's discarded charge.
why: Energy (facts 8, 10): recovers ~25-40% of bitline activation energy, the largest term in random-access energy.

title: Impact-ionization latches sense at a 0.4 V array voltage
idea: Ideal result: CV^2 near zero because the array runs at a fraction of a volt. Build the SA cross-coupled pair from impact-ionization MOS devices whose sub-5 mV/decade switching regenerates full logic levels from a 0.4 V supply, letting VARY drop from ~1 V.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline energy scales with V^2, so ~6x less array energy at 0.4 V if the cell holds enough charge.

title: Light-driven wordlines turn the decoder into an optical pattern
idea: Ideal result: addressing at light speed with no decoder transistors. A photonic layer above the array carries waveguides with grating taps over each sub-wordline driver; a photoconductive switch fires the driver only when its waveguide-wavelength pair is lit, with decoding done by an off-array laser and arrayed-waveguide router.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and energy: row decoders and global wordline wiring shrink to waveguides; fJ-class addressing energy.

title: Processor-hosted sense amps make memory dies pure cell fabric
idea: Ideal result: the memory die holds nothing but bits. Hybrid-bond a cell-only die face-to-face onto the accelerator die, which carries all sense amps, decoders and row buffers in advanced logic at ~1 um bond pitch, so data never crosses a PHY.
why: Facts 5, 7: memory die area per bit drops ~45% and data movement falls to ~0.1 pJ/bit; the cell fab needs no periphery process.

title: Dithered sense amps detect signals smaller than their offset
idea: Ideal result: a sense amp immune to its own noise. Inject controlled random dither into the SA reference and fire 8 fast mini-decisions on the shared bitline; majority counting extracts signals well below the static offset (stochastic resonance).
why: Charge wall (fact 1): allows ~2-3x smaller Cs at modest latency cost, suitable for capacity-tier memory.

title: Time-domain sensing converts bitline signal into delay
idea: Ideal result: sensing that improves with digital scaling, not analog headroom. Each bitline drives a current-starved inverter whose delay depends on its voltage; a column-shared time-to-digital converter decides the bit and also reports margin or multi-level information in the same pass.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): time resolution improves each node while voltage headroom does not; works below 0.6 V supplies.

title: Neighbor bitlines form a SAR DAC for two-bit cells
idea: Ideal result: the bitline itself is the analog-to-digital converter. Store 4 charge levels per cell and resolve them by successive approximation, with adjacent precharged bitlines switched in binary-weighted groups acting as the DAC capacitors against the sensed line.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits/cell at ~1.3x periphery cost gives ~1.5x bits per wafer without a litho shrink (fact 4).

title: Shift-token wordlines replace decoders for streaming AI weights
idea: Ideal result: no address decoding because the next row is always known. For weight-streaming tiers, chain sub-wordline drivers into a shift register so a single token ripples row to row; only stream entry points use a coarse decoder.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): row decoders shrink ~80% in streaming mats; inference reads weights sequentially, so random row access is rarely needed.

title: Analog activation integrators in wordline drivers stop row hammer
idea: Ideal result: a row that knows when its neighbors are in danger. Each sub-wordline driver adds a fixed charge quantum to a tiny leaky capacitor per activation; crossing a comparator threshold flags a targeted neighbor refresh, and the leak resets it at the refresh-window rate.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2% driver area instead of counter SRAM or 10-15% bandwidth for probabilistic schemes.

title: Ferroelectric polarization kick boosts wordlines without charge pumps
idea: Ideal result: a 3 V wordline from a 1 V supply with no pump. A ferroelectric capacitor at each wordline driver output releases its remanent charge (~20-40 uC/cm^2) on polarization switching, bootstrapping the wordline above the supply locally.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): removes VPP charge pumps (several % die area and ~30% pump efficiency loss).

title: Refresh stream doubles as a free read channel
idea: Ideal result: reading costs nothing because the row is already open. Route rows opened by refresh into an on-die staging buffer and serve queued reads to that row from it, while the scheduler reorders refresh to hit predicted hot rows first.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3, 8): turns part of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss into useful bandwidth, up to ~10% effective gain.

title: Completion-detecting sense amps make access time average, not worst case
idea: Ideal result: a read that takes exactly as long as that bit needs. Each SA stripe adds a done-detector on replica latches that signals when regeneration completes; the controller uses an asynchronous handshake instead of a fixed worst-case tRCD.
why: Latency and bandwidth: typical cells have ~2x margin over the worst case, so average tRCD falls ~30%.

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor charging cuts wordline drive energy
idea: Ideal result: wordlines that swing 3 V for free. Drive each global wordline through 4-6 staircase steps from on-die tank capacitors at intermediate voltages, so each step dissipates only (dV)^2 and charge returns to the tanks on the falling edge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline swing energy drops ~3-5x and charge pump load falls accordingly.

title: Socketed HBM base die rescues good DRAM dies from failed stacks
idea: Ideal result: a stack that is never scrapped. Join the periphery/base logic die to the DRAM stack with low-temperature indium micro-bumps and a removable clamp frame instead of underfill, so a failed base die or bad bottom joint is swapped at ~160 C and the good DRAM dies are reused.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss; the base die becomes a field-replaceable part.

title: Laser-release bond layers let one bad tier be swapped
idea: Ideal result: a 3D memory whose layers come apart like building blocks. Insert a thin UV-absorbing release layer in each cell-on-periphery tier bond, so laser lift-off separates a failing tier and a known-good tier is re-bonded onto the same periphery.
why: 3D DRAM yield compounds per tier (fact 2): rework makes 26+ tiers economically tolerable and keeps the periphery tier in service.

title: Solvent-releasable spare-die patch site on every DIMM
idea: Ideal result: a module that repairs itself by accepting a spare part. Each DIMM has an empty die site using anisotropic conductive film; when a die fails, a depot bonds a spare there and the register clock driver remaps that die's chip-select to it, and the film later dissolves for reclaim.
why: Usable supply: keeps 95%+ of module bits in service instead of scrapping whole DIMMs during a shortage.

title: Wafer-scale memory board with pick-and-place replaceable cell tiles
idea: Ideal result: memory as a field of interchangeable tiles. A periphery interposer wafer carries all decoders and sense amps in repeated sockets; small cell-array tiles are compression-bonded, tested in place, and bad tiles are lifted and replaced.
why: Yield and capital (facts 4, 7): tiny tiles yield ~99%, and the periphery wafer can be built at 28-40 nm in the U.S.

title: Error-correcting address codes keep decoders working after faults
idea: Ideal result: a decoder that cannot misfire. Encode each row address into a distance-3 code across the predecode lines, so a stuck predecode wire or broken gate still selects the correct row (or none, never two), and the fault is reported for repair.
why: Periphery reliability (fact 7): decoder faults become repairable events instead of yield or field killers.

title: Atom-switch rewiring makes decoder redundancy field-reprogrammable
idea: Ideal result: wiring that can be redrawn after shipment. Place Cu-ion bridge (atom) switches in the BEOL between decoder outputs and spare wordline drivers; a field repair command forms or dissolves bridges to remap any row to any spare, repeatedly.
why: Repair: replaces one-shot laser or e-fuses with reversible rewiring, extending module life and salvaging aging parts.

title: One roving spare sense amp covers any failed column
idea: Ideal result: one spare that is everywhere. A single fast spare SA per mat is time-shared through a column steering bus with per-column sample capacitors; when built-in self-test finds a dead SA, the spare substitutes, and its assignment moves as new faults appear.
why: Repair cost: cuts redundant-column area overhead ~3-5x versus fixed spare columns.

title: Weak rows convert to twin-cell mode on the fly
idea: Ideal result: aging cells heal by teaming up. The row decoder can tie two physical rows into one logical row storing true and complement, so the SA sees a 2x differential signal; rows failing retention are downgraded to twin mode instead of being fused out.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3) and repair: rescues weak rows at a local 50% capacity cost and lets the whole die run a longer refresh period.

title: On-die microheaters anneal aging sense amps back to health
idea: Ideal result: periphery that resets its own wear. Polysilicon microheaters under SA stripes and drivers heat local transistors to ~250 C for seconds during maintenance windows, recovering BTI and hot-carrier threshold shifts.
why: Lifetime and offset (facts 1, 7): keeps SA offsets near day-zero for years, allowing tighter margins and longer service life.

title: Polarity-swapping latches spread transistor stress evenly
idea: Ideal result: transistors that never age unevenly. Periodically invert each mat's stored polarity, tracked by one inversion flag bit, so every SA cross-coupled pair sees balanced BTI stress and offset drift never accumulates.
why: Offset drift otherwise eats ~5-10 mV of margin over life; recovered margin allows smaller Cs and longer service.

title: Double-ended sub-wordline drivers survive any single driver failure
idea: Ideal result: a wordline that cannot be cut off. Drive each sub-wordline from both ends with drivers that can be disabled individually; if self-test finds one dead or a mid-line break, the other end drives the line.
why: Removes a top cause of row fuse-outs and halves wordline RC delay, enabling longer wordlines and fewer driver stripes (fact 7).

title: ECC syndromes trigger background column remapping
idea: Ideal result: a memory that fixes faults before anyone notices. On-die ECC logs syndromes per column in a small nonvolatile table; repeat offenders are remapped to spare columns online, with data copied during refresh idle time.
why: Keeps parts in service and cuts module returns; periphery repair happens continuously in the field.

title: Second-life re-binning retunes sensing on retired server DIMMs
idea: Ideal result: no DIMM ever goes to the shredder. A depot tester sweeps each retired module's per-bank tRCD, tWR and refresh margins, writes a custom timing and refresh profile into its SPD, and resells it into edge, client and cache tiers.
why: Usable supply: extends module life 3-5 years, adding supply during a 4x price spike at near-zero capital.

title: Reusable donor wafers supply periphery silicon via layer transfer
idea: Ideal result: silicon that is used ten times. Grow periphery device layers on a porous-silicon or SiGe release substrate, transfer the thin layer onto the bonded memory stack, then polish and reuse the donor wafer.
why: Scarce resources: cuts virgin wafer and Spruce Pine quartz crucible demand for periphery tiers ~5-10x.

title: Tungsten-free periphery metal designed for selective recovery
idea: Ideal result: periphery made only of materials you can get back. Replace W contacts and wordline straps with Mo and Ru using liner chemistries chosen for selective wet dissolution, so end-of-life dies yield separable Cu, Mo and Ru streams.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and recyclability by design.

title: Open sense-interface standard makes periphery dies universal and reusable
idea: Ideal result: any cell array plugs into any periphery. Define a bond-level standard (bitline pitch, timing, trim protocol) between cell dies and periphery dies, so U.S.-made periphery dies work with multiple cell fabs and can be re-bonded to the next array generation.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: periphery made on mature U.S. nodes, cell dies dual-sourced, periphery reusable across generations.

title: HBM buyback harvests base dies and good DRAM layers
idea: Ideal result: every die returns to service. Vendors pay a deposit-refund on HBM-equipped modules; returned stacks with reversible bonds are disassembled, dies retested, and good DRAM layers restacked onto new base dies.
why: Supply and capital: recovers bits at a fraction of new-wafer cost and offsets HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit (fact 6).

title: Right-to-repair rule exposing spare rows to operators
idea: Ideal result: owners fix memory themselves. Require DRAM to expose a standard post-package repair command set, spare-row counts and repair logs to the OS, so data centers repair faults in place rather than return modules.
why: Usable supply: fewer discarded modules; a low-cost policy lever during the shortage.

title: Trim storage on the cell die makes periphery dies generic
idea: Ideal result: the periphery die carries no identity. Store all array-specific trims (redundancy map, reference offsets) in a small ferroelectric block on the cell die instead of periphery e-fuses, so periphery dies are tested generically and can be re-bonded to any array.
why: Enables periphery rebonding and recycling and removes fuse banks from the periphery die (fact 7).

title: Liquid-metal capsules self-heal broken vertical interconnects
idea: Ideal result: a broken wire that rejoins itself. Fill spare vias beside TSVs and bitline contacts with encapsulated Ga-In micro-capsules that rupture from the local heat of a forming void and wick into the crack, restoring continuity.
why: TSV yield (fact 6) and lifetime reliability: converts open-circuit failures into self-repairs.

title: OS-visible elastic capacity retires failed mats instead of modules
idea: Ideal result: memory that degrades by grams, not kilograms. Periphery reports failed or weak mats through a standard interface, and the OS offlines just those address ranges, shrinking capacity by a fraction of a percent per fault.
why: Keeps modules in service for years, raising usable supply.

title: Retired sense-amp stripes reborn as bit-serial compute engines
idea: Ideal result: periphery that finds a second job. Design SA stripes with a bit-serial logic mode (multi-row activation for AND/OR plus a latch-side XOR), so dies retired for poor retention are reused as in-memory compute engines with short data lifetimes.
why: Recyclability: a second-life market for degraded dies, and fewer data-movement joules (fact 5) for bulk bitwise work.

title: Off-die replaceable voltage-generation chiplet powers memory periphery
idea: Ideal result: the memory die holds no pumps or regulators that wear out. Move VPP, VBB and VARY generation to a socketed power chiplet on the module that feeds dies through dedicated rails; failing or outdated regulators are swapped, and the chiplet is reused on new modules.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): frees several percent of die area from charge pumps and makes the highest-stress periphery repairable.
